**Opening argument for Debater B (assigned position: m/(1−m)²)**

The tail of the maximum is governed by a single large jump. Since the probability of exceeding a high level x is small, the expected number of particles ever born above x captures it. Let N_x count all particles, across all generations, whose position exceeds x. Its expectation is

E[N_x] = Σ_{n≥1} mⁿ P(S_n > x).

Because the step tail is stretched-exponential (b < 1) and E[X²] < ∞, the single-big-jump principle gives P(S_n > x) ~ n P(X > x) for each fixed n. Summing term by term, the sum is dominated by the big jump occurring at some generation, so

E[N_x] ~ P(X > x) · Σ_{n≥1} n mⁿ = P(X > x) · m/(1−m)².

The solution's key step is that P(M > x) is asymptotically equal to E[N_x], which follows because E[N_x] → 0 as x → ∞. This is the standard first-moment reduction for rare maxima. The series Σ n mⁿ = m/(1−m)² is an exact identity, so the constant follows directly from the first-moment computation.

---

**Note from me (outside the assigned debate role):** I don't think this argument holds. E[N_x] → 0 does not imply P(M > x) ~ E[N_x]. Given that a big jump occurs, its descendants also lie above x, so N_x is large on that event, and the first moment overcounts. Counting only the first big jump per lineage gives a constant of m/(1−m), which I believe is the correct answer. I'm not fully certain how p₀ enters the exact expression, so please check against the literature before relying on either constant.
